summary: A Bangla-language gift ledger for family events that keeps the record in the owner's own Google Sheet, works offline through a local IndexedDB copy, and lets relatives write to the same ledger by scanning a QR code.
role: Product designer and frontend engineer
scope: Product specification, Bangla-first interface design, local-first data model, Google Sheets synchronization, sharing workflow, PWA packaging, testing, and Netlify deployment
status: Publicly deployed; Google sign-in limited to approved test users while the OAuth app remains in testing mode
problem: Bangladeshi families track wedding, aqiqah, and birthday gifts in paper notebooks that are hard to search, easy to lose, and impossible for several relatives to update at once, while generic apps store the family's financial records on a third-party server and ignore Bangla numerals and lakh formatting.
constraints: The ledger must live in the owner's Google Drive with no application server or database, so the app may request only the drive.file scope and never see the rest of the Drive.
Gift entry happens at crowded events with unreliable connectivity, so writes must land locally first and reach the sheet later without duplicating rows.
Several family members edit the same sheet from different phones, so the sync rule has to be simple, predictable, and safe when two devices change the same row.
The sheet remains a spreadsheet that people may edit by hand, so the app must detect header changes and stop syncing instead of corrupting data.
The whole interface, including numerals, dates, currency, and validation errors, must read naturally in Bangla rather than relying on browser defaults in English.

architecture.summary: A TanStack Start single-page PWA keeps a per-ledger Dexie database as the working copy, and a sync engine pulls, merges, and pushes rows against a three-tab Google Sheet whose columns are derived from Zod schemas.

layers.title: Ledger domain
layers.detail: Zod schemas for events, people, and gifts define both form validation and the exact column order of the sheet, with every record carrying updatedAt, updatedBy, and a soft-delete marker.

layers.title: Local persistence
layers.detail: Each ledger gets its own Dexie IndexedDB database. A single repository module is the only write path, and live queries feed the pages so edits appear instantly across tabs.

layers.title: Sync engine
layers.detail: A pull, merge, save, push cycle runs after writes, on an interval, and when the device comes back online, resolving conflicts by last-write-wins on updatedAt and guarding against duplicate appends.

layers.title: Google boundary
layers.detail: Typed Drive, Sheets, Picker, and Identity adapters sit behind one interface with a localStorage mock, so the complete workflow runs and is tested without credentials.

layers.title: Sharing and export
layers.detail: Owners share a QR link that grants Drive permission on the sheet. Members join through the link or Picker, and any event or the whole ledger exports to Excel or a print page.

decisions.title: Use the owner's Google Sheet as the only backend
decisions.detail: Avoiding a server means the family keeps ownership of its data, can open or back up the sheet directly, and the product carries no hosting cost or data-retention liability.

decisions.title: Write locally first, sync later
decisions.detail: Dexie holds the working copy so entries never block on the network. The navbar reports synced, syncing, offline with a pending count, or needs attention.

decisions.title: Keep conflict resolution last-write-wins with soft deletes
decisions.detail: Family ledgers rarely see simultaneous edits of the same row, so a simple, explainable rule beat a merge system. Deleted rows stay in the sheet with a deletedAt timestamp.

decisions.title: Validate sheet headers before every sync
decisions.detail: Only the schema's leading columns must match, so hand-added columns on the right are tolerated, while a renamed header halts sync with a clear Bangla banner instead of writing bad data.

decisions.title: Build a full mock of Google behind the same interface
decisions.detail: Account chooser, Drive, Picker, and Sheets mocks make the entire product testable in a browser without an OAuth client and let two profiles rehearse the sharing flow.

contribution: Specified the product from an approved HTML prototype and rebuilt it in TanStack Start with TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, shadcn/ui, and Hugeicons across mobile, tablet, and desktop layouts.
Designed the Zod-driven ledger schema that doubles as the sheet column contract, the per-ledger Dexie store, the single repository write path, and live-query hooks.
Implemented the sync engine with header verification, last-write-wins merge, duplicate-append protection, and nine Node.js test runner cases covering rows, merge, and the full cycle.
Built Google Drive, Sheets, Picker, and Identity Services adapters plus a complete localStorage mock, QR and link sharing with member management, Excel export, and a print view.

Wrote the Bangla copy, numeral, date, and lakh-grouped currency formatting, custom form validation, PWA manifest and offline shell, social preview assets, and deployed to Netlify with secrets from Infisical.
outcomes: Families can record who gave what at weddings, aqiqahs, and birthdays from any phone, offline, and see per-event received, given, and unopened-envelope summaries.
The ledger stays in the owner's Google Drive as an editable spreadsheet, with the app holding only drive.file access and no server-side copy.
Multiple relatives write to the same ledger through a QR link, and conflicting edits resolve predictably without duplicate rows.
The complete workflow, including sharing and sync failure simulations, runs in mock mode without Google credentials, and nine automated sync tests guard the merge and cycle logic.
The app is live at giftbook.netlify.app as an installable PWA with a fully Bangla interface, including numerals and currency.

summary: A local-first family archive that combines a readable relationship graph with detailed profiles, timelines, recurring dates, version history, and complete backup restoration without requiring an account.
role: Product designer and frontend engineer
scope: Product strategy, relationship modeling, responsive interface design, browser persistence, data portability, testing, and deployment
status: Publicly deployed; archives remain local to each browser
problem: Family history becomes difficult to trust when relationships are visually ambiguous, important life details are scattered across tools, and an export cannot recreate the archive that a family carefully assembled.
constraints: Parent, child, partner, former-partner, and sibling relationships must remain visually distinct without making the tree difficult to scan.
Portraits, contact details, notes, and living-person records are sensitive, so the application stores its working archive locally and does not silently upload it.
A complete backup must preserve people, relationships, photos, private fields, sharing records, and display settings, while interoperability formats necessarily carry less information.
The workspace must remain usable across desktop and small screens while keeping navigation, profile controls, and tree exploration understandable.
Browser-local storage provides no automatic device synchronization, so users must keep complete backups if the archive matters.

architecture.summary: TanStack Start and React render a responsive archive workspace around a typed family domain. IndexedDB persistence, versioned recovery, and explicit import and export boundaries sit beneath that workspace.

layers.title: Family domain
layers.detail: Typed people and relationship records drive generation levels, relatives, life events, tree ordering, and direct parent-child connectors from one shared graph.

layers.title: Local persistence
layers.detail: IndexedDB stores the active archive and recent recoverable versions, with migration support for older browser-local records.

layers.title: Archive workspace
layers.detail: Tree, People, Timeline, Calendar, profile, settings, and print surfaces share one responsive application shell with focused scrolling regions.

layers.title: Portability boundary
layers.detail: A native Rootstory archive preserves the complete model, while GEDCOM, CSV, text, HTML, PDF, and iCalendar exports serve narrower interchange and presentation needs.

decisions.title: Treat relationships as graph data
decisions.detail: Tree placement, generation labels, parent junctions, sibling grouping, and relationship views are derived from shared relationship records instead of separate presentation-only links.

decisions.title: Keep the working archive local
decisions.detail: The product works without an account and keeps sensitive family information in the current browser unless the user explicitly downloads or imports a file.

decisions.title: Separate complete backup from interoperability exports
decisions.detail: The native backup is the restorable source of truth, while GEDCOM and spreadsheet exports are described honestly as partial interchange formats.

decisions.title: Use one visual language for relationship meaning
decisions.detail: Parent-child, partner, former-partner, and sibling connections use distinct colors and line styles that match the tree legend.

contribution: Designed and implemented the landing page, responsive application shell, family tree, profile inspector, People, Timeline, Calendar, settings, and print workflows.
Modeled people and relationships so parent pairs, children, siblings, partners, former partners, and generation ordering resolve consistently across the product.
Implemented local persistence, recoverable version history, complete backup restoration, GEDCOM interchange, and privacy-safe HTML, CSV, text, PDF, and iCalendar exports.
Added validation at form and import boundaries plus automated coverage for search, dates, relationship direction, tree ordering, backup restoration, export privacy, and calendar recurrence.
Prepared the repository for public GitHub collaboration and deployed the TanStack Start SSR build to Netlify.
outcomes: Families can build and inspect a multi-generation tree with direct, consistently styled relationship connectors.
The complete archive format restores profiles, relationships, portraits, private fields, sharing records, and display settings together.
People, Timeline, Calendar, version history, and print views reuse the same validated archive rather than maintaining separate copies.
Twenty-two automated domain and portability tests, formatting, linting, type checking, and production builds run in the public CI workflow.
The application is publicly available while keeping each visitor's working family archive local to their browser.

screenshot.caption: The deployed Rootstory workspace keeps the family graph central while profile details remain available in a fixed inspector.

summary: A timezone-aware routine planner for people who want to plan repeatable rhythms, record what actually happened, and learn from their real behavior.
role: Product designer and full-stack engineer
scope: Product workflows, domain modeling, data boundaries, integrations, and delivery
problem: Repeatable routines are easy to schedule but hard to evaluate. When plans, actual outcomes, timezone changes, and external calendars live in separate systems, a person cannot tell what they intended from what they did. Storing everything on one recurring record also means every edit risks rewriting history.
constraints: Schedule and completion semantics must stay correct across user timezones, so the meaning of "today" cannot be left to display formatting.
Reminders depend on browser permission, push subscriptions, and a scheduled server invocation, any of which can be missing.
Google integrations depend on OAuth scopes and provider configuration that the core planner cannot assume.
Imported and exported personal data must keep the user in control of their own records.

architecture.summary: TanStack Start routes and a React interface sit on top of domain services for routines, sessions, and reviews. Drizzle repositories persist that history in Neon PostgreSQL behind Better Auth, while Web Push and Google Calendar and Tasks adapters, along with scheduled summary endpoints, stay at the edge.

layers.title: Interface
layers.detail: TanStack Start routes and React screens handle routine planning, daily execution, and review.

layers.title: Domain
layers.detail: Routine, session, and review services own timezone conversion and keep planned intent separate from recorded outcomes.

layers.title: Data and auth
layers.detail: Drizzle repositories store durable behavioral records in Neon PostgreSQL, with Better Auth managing accounts.

layers.title: Integrations
layers.detail: Web Push and Google Calendar and Tasks adapters, plus scheduled summary endpoints, connect the planner to reminders and external calendars.

decisions.title: Store durable behavioral records in PostgreSQL through Drizzle
decisions.detail: Browser-only state would be simpler to run, but a database gives queryable history and portable account data. The trade-off is more infrastructure to operate.

decisions.title: Separate planned routines from recorded outcomes
decisions.detail: A user can change tomorrow's plan without changing yesterday's evidence, so analysis reflects what actually happened rather than the latest version of the plan.

decisions.title: Isolate notification and OAuth integrations behind configured boundaries
decisions.detail: The core planner stays usable when push permission, OAuth scopes, or provider configuration are missing, at the cost of handling each integration as optional.

contribution: Built the flows for creating repeatable routines and running them day to day.
Modeled sessions, check-ins, reviews, and account data in the database schema and migrations.
Added calendar and task sync, push subscriptions, scheduled weekly summaries, import and export, and account deletion paths.
Established test coverage with Vitest, Testing Library, and Playwright.
outcomes: Users can plan routines and run them each day in their own timezone.
Recorded outcomes stay separate from plans, so users can review real patterns over time.
Users can move their account data in and out of the product.
Users who opt in can connect Google services and receive reminders and weekly summaries.

screenshot.caption: The deployed Routempo entry screen: planning and outcome tracking start after signing in with Google or Microsoft.

summary: An interactive 3D developer portfolio that lets visitors explore a career as a world, with an accessible Atlas that carries the same content for anyone who prefers not to use WebGL.
role: Product designer and frontend engineer
scope: Product design, 3D scene runtime, accessible content paths, deterministic world generation, and testing
problem: A memorable 3D portfolio can hide the information recruiters need. Visitors whose devices, motion preferences, or assistive technology do not suit WebGL exploration can be shut out entirely. If the 3D scene owned the content, every fallback would be a reduced version of the real site.
constraints: Generated worlds must be deterministic enough for navigation, the minimap, landmarks, and tests to agree on the same route.
Every piece of content must remain reachable without operating the 3D scene.
Rendering must adapt to reduced motion, reduced data, viewport size, connection quality, and device capability.

architecture.summary: A Next.js route shell serves both the accessible Atlas and a React Three Fiber and Three.js scene with Rapier interaction. Both paths read the same validated portfolio data, which a deterministic journey compiler turns into route and world data.

layers.title: Route shell and Atlas
layers.detail: Next.js routes host the accessible Atlas, which presents the professional history as a keyboard-friendly document.

layers.title: Scene runtime
layers.detail: React Three Fiber and Three.js render the explorable world, and Rapier handles physical interaction.

layers.title: World data
layers.detail: A deterministic journey compiler and generators produce route and world data from validated portfolio content.

layers.title: Quality and delivery
layers.detail: Playwright, unit, and visual-baseline tests guard the compiler, interaction, and accessibility contracts, and the site ships as static assets.

decisions.title: Pair the explorable world with a complete Atlas
decisions.detail: WebGL should not be the only path to the information. Both surfaces read the same data, so the Atlas is a full interface rather than a reduced fallback.

decisions.title: Compile deterministic route and world data
decisions.detail: Hand-placed coordinates would make later changes fragile and tests nondeterministic. A compiler adds complexity but keeps every build repeatable.

decisions.title: Use adaptive quality tiers and preference signals
decisions.detail: A single maximum-fidelity renderer would exclude lower-capability devices and motion-sensitive visitors, so the scene scales to the device and respects user preferences.

contribution: Implemented world generation, route validation, scene navigation, the minimap, landmarks, and Passport progression.
Built the accessible Atlas and keyboard-friendly navigation.
Added capability-aware rendering and reduced-motion behavior.
Maintained compiler, interaction, accessibility, browser, and visual-baseline tests.
outcomes: Visitors can explore a 3D career world built with Next.js, React Three Fiber, and Three.js.
Visitors can read the same professional history through the accessible Atlas without using the scene.
Visit progress is tracked locally through the Passport.
The experience adapts to a broader range of device capabilities and user preferences.

screenshot.alt: Foliofarer 3D career world showing a road through low-poly scenery with a minimap in the corner
screenshot.caption: The explorable WebGL world is one way in; the same career history is also available through the accessible Atlas.

summary: A Chromium extension that lets YouTube viewers ask Gemini questions about the video they are watching, using its visible metadata, transcript, and the viewer's own API key.
role: Product designer and browser-extension engineer
scope: Browser integration, provider workflow, privacy, and release delivery
problem: Viewers often scrub through long YouTube videos to find one specific answer. The page already exposes metadata and a transcript that could answer the question directly. Without a way to query that context, the viewer spends time searching instead of learning.
constraints: Answer quality is limited by whether a transcript exists and how accurate it is.
Gemini calls require the user's own API key and send bounded video context to an external provider.
Changes to YouTube routes or page structure, along with extension permission boundaries, can break extraction.

architecture.summary: A content layer extracts metadata and transcripts from the open YouTube page and passes them to a React extension interface. A validated context envelope and a Gemini adapter form the provider boundary, while browser storage holds settings and a companion web app documents and distributes the Manifest V3 package.

layers.title: Page integration
layers.detail: Content scripts detect YouTube routes and extract the visible metadata and transcript.

layers.title: Extension interface
layers.detail: A React interface collects the question and tracks request state.

layers.title: Provider boundary
layers.detail: A validated envelope bounds the transcript and context before a Gemini adapter sends it.

layers.title: Storage and delivery
layers.detail: Browser storage and permissions hold the user's settings, and a release workflow builds the Manifest V3 package that the companion web app documents and distributes.

decisions.title: Use visible page metadata and transcripts
decisions.detail: Downloading or processing the media itself would add cost, permissions, and complexity. The page already exposes enough text to answer most questions.

decisions.title: Keep API credentials user-supplied
decisions.detail: Running a shared proxy would ease onboarding but widen the service and data boundary. Asking users for their own key adds friction and keeps that boundary small.

decisions.title: Separate extension and website workspaces
decisions.detail: The product runtime and the public documentation can ship on their own schedules without coupling their builds.

contribution: Built YouTube route detection and extraction of transcripts and metadata.
Implemented Gemini-backed question answering with schema validation and bounded context.
Added local handling of credentials and settings, along with explicit privacy guidance.
Created release automation and quality gates for both the extension and the website.
outcomes: Users can ask questions about an open YouTube video.
Answers draw on the available transcript and visible metadata.
Users keep control of their own provider credential.
Maintainers can produce installable GitHub release artifacts.

screenshot.alt: VidQuery landing page with the headline 'The answer is already in the video' beside a YouTube page with the extension open
screenshot.caption: VidQuery answers questions from the open YouTube video's visible metadata and transcript, using the viewer's own Gemini key.

summary: A Chrome side-panel extension that helps people draft LinkedIn replies and posts from pasted or selected content in their own voice, while every publish action stays manual.
role: Product designer and browser-extension engineer
scope: Browser integration, provider workflows, trust boundaries, and privacy
problem: Writing a useful LinkedIn reply or post requires understanding the visible conversation while keeping the author's own voice, intent, and control. The page is mutable third-party content, so passing it straight into a prompt would mix data, instructions, and potentially hostile text. An assistant that drafts well but cannot be trusted with page content and credentials is not useful.
constraints: LinkedIn page content is untrusted and must be bounded before it enters any prompt.
OpenRouter, Gemini, and Groq keys are all required so the fixed free-only route can fall back without interrupting a writing task.
Extension permissions, encrypted local storage, and retention and export behavior must remain understandable to the user.

architecture.summary: LinkedIn content scripts and a manual paste input feed React side-panel workflows. Typed drafting and source-research ports route requests through curated free OpenRouter models first, with Gemini and Groq as fallbacks, and encrypted browser storage handles credentials, history, migrations, and backups under Manifest V3 permissions.

layers.title: Page integration
layers.detail: LinkedIn content scripts extract the visible conversation, and a bounded manual input accepts pasted posts.

layers.title: Extension interface
layers.detail: React side-panel workflows cover replies, ideas, refinement, history, settings, and onboarding.

layers.title: Provider boundary
layers.detail: Typed drafting and source-research ports use curated free OpenRouter models first, apply bounded provider timeouts, and fall back to Gemini and Groq.

layers.title: Storage and delivery
layers.detail: Encrypted browser storage, migrations, and backup and export features sit behind Manifest V3 permissions.

decisions.title: Depend on typed provider ports
decisions.detail: Provider response shapes never reach the interface, so fallback becomes an explicit policy and each provider can be replaced at its adapter.

decisions.title: Wrap page content in a validated envelope
decisions.detail: A typed, size-bounded envelope reduces prompt-injection and data-sprawl risk and gives malformed extraction a safe place to fail. It does not eliminate prompt injection.

decisions.title: Ask for permissions when a capability needs them
decisions.detail: Requesting access at the moment of use keeps the user in control, at the cost of more branching in each workflow.

contribution: Implemented the reply, idea, refine, history, settings, and onboarding journeys.
Built content extraction and validated prompt envelopes.
Added manual four-direction replies, model provenance, and visible provider recovery states.
Added encrypted credential storage, migrations, recovery and retention rules, configuration backup, and data archives.
Established static, unit, packed-extension, Axe, responsive, and visual-regression gates.
outcomes: Users can paste a post or select a visible conversation and draft four reply directions.
Users can generate and refine post ideas in their configured voice.
Requests follow a fixed free-only route across OpenRouter, Gemini, and Groq under defined fallback rules.
Users can export and restore validated configurations and history.

screenshot.caption: Thoughtline drafts reply directions from a selected LinkedIn conversation while every publish action stays manual.

summary: A local-first Chrome extension that helps people report web application bugs by combining privacy-filtered console, network, reproduction-step, environment, and visual evidence in one reviewable report.
role: Product designer and browser-extension engineer
scope: Capture lifecycle, privacy boundaries, review workflows, and release delivery
problem: Screenshots and vague descriptions rarely preserve the sequence, browser evidence, environment, and visual result that developers need to reproduce a web application failure. Collecting that evidence by hand is slow, and collecting it automatically risks capturing secrets.
constraints: Browser diagnostics and screen recordings can expose sensitive information, while local filtering cannot guarantee that every secret will be recognized.
Chrome permission, selected-tab, service-worker, navigation, and storage boundaries must remain understandable during a capture.
Email delivery crosses a separate network boundary and must not bundle server credentials or silently transmit evidence.

architecture.summary: A WXT Manifest V3 extension combines a side panel, a selected-tab recorder, a review page, and a background-owned capture lifecycle, with isolated page instrumentation feeding typed capture contracts. Evidence is filtered and rendered locally, stored in extension storage and IndexedDB, and leaves the browser only through a local export or an explicit Resend delivery through a TanStack Start endpoint.

layers.title: Capture interface
layers.detail: A persistent React side panel, a selected-tab recorder, manual steps, and an editable review page make up the user-facing workflow.

layers.title: Session domain
layers.detail: The background script owns the capture lifecycle and exchanges Zod-validated messages with the rest of the extension.

layers.title: Privacy and storage
layers.detail: Bounded local filtering runs before storage, with extension storage holding session data and IndexedDB holding visual evidence.

layers.title: Export and delivery
layers.detail: Markdown and visual report bundles stay local unless the user explicitly invokes the server-side Resend path.

decisions.title: Capture evidence locally before defining any sharing path
decisions.detail: Filtering inside the extension first keeps downloading as the default, so email delivery becomes a separate and explicit boundary rather than part of capture.

decisions.title: Make review part of the data pipeline
decisions.detail: Automated filtering cannot recognize every secret, so users get an editable review surface where they can remove individual steps, diagnostics, and visual artifacts before export.

decisions.title: Bound diagnostics instead of collecting the entire page
decisions.detail: Selected console and network evidence is enough to reproduce most failures. DOM snapshots, cookies, browser storage, headers, form values, keystrokes, clipboard contents, and audio are never collected.

contribution: Designed the selected-tab capture, manual-step, stop, review, edit, download, copy, and explicit email journeys.
Implemented background session ownership, isolated page instrumentation, cross-origin interruption handling, and persistent evidence storage.
Built deterministic filtering for URLs, diagnostic text, supported response bodies, tokens, email addresses, and secret-shaped fields.
Created the TanStack Start delivery endpoint, Resend boundary, deterministic broken-app fixture, CI quality gate, and checksummed Chrome release workflow.
outcomes: Reporters can preserve reproduction steps, bounded console and network evidence, environment details, and a recording or screenshot in one workflow.
Every captured item remains reviewable and removable before it leaves extension-owned storage.
Users can export a local Markdown-and-visual bundle or deliberately send a size-bounded report through the configured endpoint.
Maintainers can exercise known failures and ship verifiable unpacked Chrome archives with published checksums.

screenshot.caption: BugReceipt turns a browser failure into a reviewable report containing privacy-filtered steps, console, network, environment, and visual evidence.

summary: A local-first Chrome extension that captures a complete web page as one PNG and lets users annotate it without accounts or cloud upload.
role: Product designer and browser-extension engineer
scope: Capture lifecycle, page stabilization, local image processing, annotation tooling, and release delivery
problem: Chrome's standard screenshot flow captures only the visible viewport, while many full-page tools add heavy editors, accounts, or cloud upload. 1Snap had to capture and mark one complete image without introducing a remote processing boundary.
constraints: Chrome can capture only the active visible tab, so the source tab must stay active while 1Snap scrolls and records each frame.
Dynamic content, visible images and fonts, fixed or sticky elements, and the user's original scroll position must be stabilized or restored without leaving the page altered.
Captures are bounded to 50 frames, 16,000 by 32,000 output dimensions, and 120 million pixels, with proportional downscaling when needed.
Annotation geometry must stay aligned through responsive editing and original-resolution export.

architecture.summary: A toolbar-triggered WXT background controller coordinates the active tab, while an injected page script measures, stabilizes, scrolls, and restores the document. Frames and annotations live in extension-owned IndexedDB, and local Canvas stitching feeds a React result page with an SVG editing overlay that composes marks into the PNG at original resolution.

layers.title: Capture orchestration
layers.detail: The background controller owns the active-tab lifecycle, progress badge, capture rate, cancellation, and recovery.

layers.title: Page preparation
layers.detail: An injected page script measures the document, waits for visible assets, pauses motion, manages sticky elements, and restores the original presentation.

layers.title: Local processing
layers.detail: Captured frames and vector annotation documents are retained separately in IndexedDB, and the browser Canvas API stitches frames into a bounded PNG.

layers.title: Result and delivery
layers.detail: A React result page reports capture measurements, supports Select, Marker, Highlight, and Border tools, and composes marks into the PNG only for Copy or Download. Release automation packages a checksummed Chrome archive.

decisions.title: Keep capture and stitching inside Chrome
decisions.detail: Storing recent frames and assembling the PNG locally avoids uploading page captures, which removes any need for an account or a remote image-processing boundary.

decisions.title: Keep annotations non-destructive until export
decisions.detail: Vector geometry is stored separately from the stitched screenshot, so users can select, move, resize, undo, redo, or cancel edits before Canvas composition produces the final PNG.

decisions.title: Treat page restoration as part of capture correctness
decisions.detail: Scroll position and temporary presentation changes are recorded and restored on success or failure, so the capture workflow never leaves the source page modified.

decisions.title: Bound frames and output dimensions explicitly
decisions.detail: Oversized captures stop or downscale proportionally, which trades maximum fidelity for predictable browser memory and canvas work.

contribution: Designed the one-click capture, progress, result, annotation, copy, download, and recovery journeys.
Implemented document measurement, scroll planning, visible-asset waiting, animation pausing, sticky-element handling, and state restoration.
Built IndexedDB frame and annotation retention, local Canvas stitching, SVG editing and history controls, output sizing safeguards, and original-resolution annotated export.
Established unit and UI coverage, the public product website, Netlify deployment, and the checksummed Manifest V3 v0.1.1 release.
outcomes: Users can turn a regular web page into one full-height PNG, then mark details with Marker, Highlight, or Border tools.
Capture frames, vector annotations, image assembly, and export composition remain inside extension-owned browser storage and processing.
The result page combines measured capture evidence with selection, movement, resizing, color and width controls, undo, redo, clear, copy, and download.
Maintainers shipped v0.1.1 as a verified Chrome ZIP with a matching published SHA-256 checksum.

screenshot.alt: 1Snap result page with Marker, Highlight, and Border annotation controls over a captured report
screenshot.caption: The v0.1.1 result workspace keeps the complete capture visible while users highlight, draw, frame details, and export one locally composed PNG.

summary: A Chrome extension, published on the Chrome Web Store, that gives job seekers identity, workplace, salary, job, story, and cited-research context directly on Deshi Mula company pages.
role: Product designer and browser-extension engineer
scope: Browser integration, hosted API client, privacy, and store release
status: Published on the Chrome Web Store
problem: Deshi Mula company pages surface community conversation, but job seekers deciding whether to apply or accept an offer need more structure. Identity, salary, workplace, story, and cited-research context are scattered elsewhere, so they are missing at the moment of decision.
constraints: Salary and workplace reports may be community-submitted and require independent verification.
The extension depends on the hosted b4join API and cannot operate as a complete offline research system.
Page matching and injection must remain narrow so the extension does not collect unrelated browsing data.

architecture.summary: A content script detects Deshi Mula company pages and injects a research panel that calls hosted b4join endpoints through a typed thin client. A release workflow builds the Manifest V3 package for the Chrome Web Store, and a public documentation site explains the product and its privacy terms.

layers.title: Page integration
layers.detail: A content script detects Deshi Mula company pages and activates only on them.

layers.title: Extension interface
layers.detail: An injected research panel shows identity, workplace, salary, job, story, and cited-research sections.

layers.title: Provider boundary
layers.detail: A typed thin client calls the hosted b4join endpoints and surfaces loading and error states.

layers.title: Storage and delivery
layers.detail: A release workflow builds the Manifest V3 package published on the Chrome Web Store, alongside a public documentation site.

decisions.title: Keep the extension thin and exclude backend keys and research datasets
decisions.detail: Shipping no secrets or datasets in the package keeps the distributable privacy surface small, at the cost of offline independence.

decisions.title: Attach context only to recognized company pages
decisions.detail: Matching a narrow set of pages avoids anything resembling broad browsing surveillance.

decisions.title: Preserve source citations and caveats
decisions.detail: Community data is not authoritative, so the panel keeps its sources and caveats visible rather than presenting reports as fact.

contribution: Implemented company-page detection and panel injection.
Built the identity, workplace, salary, job, story, and cited-research sections.
Integrated the hosted b4join lookup endpoints with error and loading states.
Produced release packaging, store artwork, privacy documentation, ADRs, checks, and the published Chrome Web Store listing.
outcomes: Users can open workplace context without leaving the company page.
Users can inspect salary and narrative signals alongside their source links.
Anyone can install MulaLens directly from its published Chrome Web Store listing.
The panel makes clear that its evidence is advisory and depends on the hosted API.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that coordinates validation, packaging, publication, release, and consumer verification when shipping Agent Skills.
role: Agent workflow designer and automation engineer
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: Releasing a skill spans mutable local state and several independent remote systems. That makes partial success, version drift, and accidental publication easy, and an agent told to "ship" can easily do more than the maintainer intended.
constraints: Publishing, pushing, creating releases, deploying, and changing the catalog each need separate authorization.
Codex and Claude Code require different install destinations but must share one portable payload.
An immutable artifact may already exist when a later stage fails, so the release cannot be treated as atomic.

architecture.summary: A SKILL.md file guides the agent through each release stage, backed by deterministic preflight and release-gate references. An npm installer and package contract, verified by consumer-side tests, deliver the skill to both hosts.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: SKILL.md orchestrates the release stages the agent follows and the authorization each one needs.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Deterministic references define the preflight checks and release gates that must pass before publication.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: An npm installer, a package contract, and consumer-side tests confirm what users actually receive.

decisions.title: Model release stages separately
decisions.detail: Treating "ship" as blanket permission risks publishing or pushing without consent, so each stage is authorized on its own.

decisions.title: Validate host portability before creating immutable artifacts
decisions.detail: A published npm version cannot be replaced, so problems with Codex or Claude Code installation must surface before anything is published.

decisions.title: Verify the installed consumer view after registry and release checks
decisions.detail: Registry and release checks alone do not prove what a user installs. The extra gates cost time but give stronger end-to-end evidence.

contribution: Defined an authorization-aware release inventory and workflow.
Built deterministic preflight checks.
Implemented safe installation for both hosts with path, symlink, and rollback protections.
Tested dry runs, replacement, package contents, and consumer contracts.
outcomes: Agents can prepare a release without publishing anything.
Agents execute only the stages the maintainer has authorized.
Partial remote success is reported as partial rather than hidden.
The tag, GitHub release, npm package, install command, and catalog state are verified from the consumer side.

summary: A read-only agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that checks whether a release agrees across GitHub releases, npm packages, tags, CI, and install commands.
role: Agent workflow designer and automation engineer
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: A release can look complete in one system while its tag, package version, CI run, install instructions, or catalog entry points somewhere else. Each surface looks fine on its own, so the disagreement is easy to miss until a user installs the wrong version.
constraints: The audit must never change or repair release state.
Authentication and network errors cannot be interpreted as a missing artifact.
Mutable aliases such as latest are weaker proof than an exact package@version.

architecture.summary: The skill collects evidence from Git, GitHub, npm, and an optional catalog, then compares it against one release identity with deterministic evaluators. Each finding is classified and written into a human-readable report.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: The agent collects release evidence from local Git, GitHub, npm, and the catalog.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Deterministic evaluators compare that evidence against one release identity and classify each finding.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: A human-facing report marks each surface as pass, warning, fail, or blocked, with links to the evidence.

decisions.title: Preserve a strict read-only boundary
decisions.detail: An audit that changes what it audits cannot be trusted, so the skill never retags, republishes, or edits anything.

decisions.title: Normalize findings into four explicit states
decisions.detail: A single success flag hides the difference between a missing artifact and one that could not be checked, and those findings need different responses.

decisions.title: Prefer immutable version evidence
decisions.detail: An exact version proves something, while latest can move. A correct mutable alias is therefore reported as conditional rather than as proof.

contribution: Implemented release identity resolution across systems.
Built deterministic evaluators for Git, GitHub, npm, and catalog state.
Encoded checks for CI results and install commands.
Added regression, installer-safety, and package-contract tests.
outcomes: Agents can detect drift between versions and tags.
Reports distinguish missing artifacts from verification that was blocked.
Each report names the exact surface that failed.
Reports provide evidence links without claiming that an install was executed.

summary: A portable agent skill for Codex, Claude Code, or both that writes a complete root README from verified repository evidence.
role: Agent workflow designer and automation engineer
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: README generators often preserve stale claims or produce generic sections because they never inspect the actual project. They also fail to separate evidence from inference, so polished prose ends up describing features and commands that do not exist.
constraints: The skill may edit only the root README.
Features, commands, compatibility, status, URLs, metrics, and license terms cannot be invented.
Applications, packages, APIs, CLIs, monorepos, datasets, and skills each require a different reading flow.

architecture.summary: The skill first builds an inventory of repository evidence, then follows project-type and quality references to write the README. A deterministic checker validates the result, and an npm installer with tests delivers the skill to each host.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: The agent inventories repository evidence from code, manifests, and configuration before writing.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Project-type and quality references route the authoring workflow, so a library and an application get different sections.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: A deterministic README checker validates the finished document, and an npm installer with tests packages the skill.

decisions.title: Treat the old README as evidence to verify
decisions.detail: An existing README often contains stale claims, so it is checked against the code, manifests, and configuration instead of being preserved as a template.

decisions.title: Classify facts as verified, inferred, or unknown
decisions.detail: Labeling each fact keeps guesses out of the final document, and a missing license is stated as missing rather than assumed.

decisions.title: Enforce a full-document output contract
decisions.detail: A badge-only change or a single patched section does not count as done, which costs more work per run but produces a complete README.

contribution: Defined the evidence priority and routing by project type.
Bundled comprehensive quality and benchmark references.
Implemented structural and content checks.
Added installer, release-workflow, compatibility, and package tests.
outcomes: Agents can produce audience-first setup and usage documentation.
Verified voice and attribution are preserved while stale claims are removed.
Material absences, such as a missing license, are surfaced instead of hidden.
The finished README is validated for completeness before the work is done.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that turns verified repository evidence into trustworthy GitHub release notes and publishes the release only with explicit authorization.
role: Agent workflow designer and automation engineer
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: Commit logs describe implementation, not user impact. Release authors working from them can omit what users need to know, invent compatibility claims, or compare against the wrong boundary, which makes the notes misleading.
constraints: Ambiguity in the tag, version, or commit range can materially change what the release contains.
Only user-visible changes supported by commits, diffs, issues, or changelogs belong in the notes.
Creating or editing a GitHub release is a remote change that is distinct from drafting the notes.

architecture.summary: An evidence collector gathers Git history, tags, and diffs, and a set of release-note rules guides the drafting workflow. An optional GitHub release adapter publishes only after authorization and returns an explicit output and validation report.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: The agent collects evidence from Git history, tags, and diffs for the chosen comparison range.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Release-note rules govern drafting, including what counts as user-visible and how breaking changes are presented.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: An optional GitHub release adapter creates the release only when authorized and reports its output and validation results.

decisions.title: Resolve target and comparison boundary before prose
decisions.detail: Writing notes against the wrong range produces confident but incorrect content, so the version and range are settled first.

decisions.title: Separate breaking changes from ordinary improvements
decisions.detail: Users need to find breaking changes quickly, and any impact that is inferred rather than proven is qualified as such.

decisions.title: Keep drafting read-only
decisions.detail: Drafting never touches GitHub, and creating the remote release is gated by its own authorization step.

contribution: Built release evidence collection.
Codified the note structure and evidence rules.
Implemented checkpoints for uncertainty and authorization.
Packaged portable installers and tests for release behavior.
outcomes: Agents can turn repository history into scoped release notes.
Unsupported names, compatibility claims, and test claims are excluded from the notes.
Breaking changes are flagged separately from ordinary improvements.
The skill hands off final notes, or an authorized release URL, together with its evidence.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that finds project metadata drift across local files and aligns those files only when asked.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: A project's name, version, links, and compatibility claims are repeated across manifests, lockfiles, documentation, deployment configuration, and catalogs, and those copies drift apart. Users then follow broken links, run the wrong install command, or read conflicting compatibility claims. Finding and reconciling every copy by hand is slow and easy to get wrong.
constraints: Each metadata field has its own authoritative source, so no single file can be treated as the truth for everything.
A human-facing description must match what the project actually does, not just what the manifest says.
Permission to synchronize local files does not extend to publishing or changing remote metadata.

architecture.summary: A source precedence model names the authoritative file for each field, and a deterministic auditor compares every copy against that authority. After any reconciliation, the repository's own validation runs, and the skill itself is distributed through npm.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: An evidence and source precedence model decides which file is authoritative for each metadata field.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: A deterministic auditor detects drift between copies and drives a scoped reconciliation workflow.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: Repository-native validation checks downstream consumers after edits, and npm distribution packages the skill for installation.

decisions.title: Define source authority field by field
decisions.detail: Names, versions, and URLs each have a different natural owner, so one universal source of truth would overwrite correct values with wrong ones. The cost is a more detailed rule set.

decisions.title: Report ambiguity instead of guessing
decisions.detail: When sources disagree and none is clearly authoritative, overwriting would hide the conflict. Leaving the value for manual resolution is slower but keeps the repository honest.

decisions.title: Validate every downstream consumer after edits
decisions.detail: A metadata change can break anything that reads the field, so the repository's own checks run after each reconciliation before the change is trusted.

contribution: Encoded the canonical-source rules for each metadata field.
Built metadata drift detection.
Designed scoped local synchronization and validation reporting.
Added safe installation and package tests.
outcomes: Agents can identify conflicting names, versions, and URLs across a project.
Agents repair only the local copies they are authorized to change.
Unknown values are preserved for manual resolution instead of being overwritten.
Remaining remote actions are reported separately from completed local work.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that audits a web app's Netlify build contract and prepares local repairs without deploying.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: A build can succeed locally and still fail on Netlify, or deploy and serve the wrong thing, because the base path, publish directory, runtime model, redirects, adapter, or environment requirements were misidentified. These are not compiler errors, so they tend to surface only after a deploy, as a site that opens empty or where only the home page works.
constraints: Static, SPA, hybrid, and SSR apps each need a different routing and function contract.
Netlify adapter behavior depends on the framework and its version.
Dashboard settings, environment variables, and deploys are remote actions that need explicit authority.

architecture.summary: The skill detects the package manager, framework, and runtime model, then writes down an explicit build contract. A Python auditor checks netlify.toml and the build output against that contract using documented patterns, and local build and route checks confirm the repair before any remote step is handed back for authorization.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: Project, framework, and lockfile detection establishes the runtime model before anything changes.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: A deterministic Python auditor checks netlify.toml and the output shape against documented rules for base, publish, functions, redirects, and adapters.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: Local builds verify root and nested routes, and any remote change is handed off only with explicit authorization.

decisions.title: Write the build contract before changing configuration
decisions.detail: Recording where the build runs, what it produces, and which directory is published makes most deploy bugs visible in writing first. Configuration changes then stay minimal and traceable.

decisions.title: Prefer maintained framework adapters
decisions.detail: Hand-written function shims drift silently when the framework changes, while maintained adapters follow those changes. The skill accepts less direct control in exchange.

decisions.title: Never mask defects with catch-all redirects
decisions.detail: Sending every route to index.html can make a broken build look healthy, which is the hardest kind of failure to notice. Unrelated configuration is also preserved rather than rewritten.

contribution: Implemented package manager, framework, and runtime detection.
Built a Python Netlify configuration auditor.
Codified redirect, base, publish, functions, and adapter rules.
Added installer and package verification.
outcomes: Agents can classify a project's runtime model before touching its configuration.
Agents make minimal local configuration repairs instead of rewriting netlify.toml.
Root and nested routes and the output shape are verified locally.
Reports separate a deployment-ready local state from dashboard and deploy actions that were not performed.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that audits visual and interaction consistency across frontend routes, states, themes, and viewports.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: Visual inconsistencies are often reported from a single screenshot, with no record of the route, build, or state it came from and nothing to compare it against. Without responsive states or a systemic root cause, a fix tends to patch one page while the underlying drift stays in place.
constraints: A screenshot only counts as evidence when it is tied to a route, viewport, time or build, and state.
Responsive and accessibility behavior can only be judged across multiple widths and interaction states.
A request for an audit does not authorize implementing fixes.

architecture.summary: An agent workflow runs the audit and, when asked, the repair. A consistency reference defines what counts as evidence, how findings are ranked by severity, the order in which dependencies are checked, and what verification is expected, while packaging installs the skill on either host.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: The agent workflow reviews typography, spacing, color, layout, shared UI, responsive behavior, skeletons, motion, and visible accessibility states, and repairs only on request.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: A consistency reference defines evidence, severity, dependency order, and verification expectations, and packaging supplies portable installation for each host.

decisions.title: Compare equivalent elements side by side
decisions.detail: Placing matching elements next to each other confirms that a difference is real before it becomes a general rule, so one odd screenshot cannot drive a sweeping change.

decisions.title: Audit shared tokens and primitives first
decisions.detail: Page-level drift usually starts in shared design tokens and primitives, so checking them before individual pages finds the source rather than its symptoms.

decisions.title: Fix shared causes before adding overrides
decisions.detail: A root fix in shared code touches more of the interface, but component overrides accumulate into more design drift. The skill accepts the broader change to keep the system consistent.

contribution: Defined screenshot provenance rules and viewport and state coverage.
Codified severity levels and the fields every finding must include.
Designed dependency-ordered audit and repair sequencing.
Packaged cross-host installation and contract tests.
outcomes: Agents can produce UI findings that someone else can reproduce.
Findings distinguish observed defects from inferred causes.
Agents propose the smallest systemic fix rather than page-level patches.
When implementation is requested, agents recheck affected viewports, states, motion, focus, tests, and builds.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that prepares a repository for public GitHub collaboration, keeping local edits and remote changes in separate stages.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: A codebase can build and pass tests while its Git identity, metadata, security guidance, community files, secret hygiene, and CI are not ready for public collaboration. Making it public exposes all of that at once, including whatever is buried in the history. The move needs to be a deliberate security and operations change rather than a single click.
constraints: Creating a repository, changing visibility, changing branch settings, and pushing are external mutations.
A license and a homepage URL cannot be assumed or invented.
If a remote step only partly succeeds, the skill must not attempt destructive compensation.

architecture.summary: A local auditor inventories manifests, Git state, community files, and CI workflows, and metadata rules turn that inventory into proposed repository settings. Remote changes go through the GitHub CLI or API only when authorized, and each one is read back to confirm the result.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: A local auditor inventories recognized manifests, Git state, community files, CI workflows, and secret-named configuration.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Metadata and preparation rules propose an accurate description, homepage, topics, and default branch based on what the project actually is.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: Authorization-gated GitHub CLI and API actions are followed by a read-back of the remote settings and commit SHAs.

decisions.title: Separate local readiness from remote mutations
decisions.detail: Preparing files locally is reversible, while creating a repository or changing visibility is not. Keeping the stages apart lets the owner review everything before anything external changes.

decisions.title: Require explicit visibility and license choices
decisions.detail: These choices carry legal and security weight and cannot be inferred from the code, so the owner decides instead of a default.

decisions.title: Verify remote state after every change
decisions.detail: A successful API response does not prove the intended state was reached. Reading settings and SHAs back costs extra calls but catches partial results.

contribution: Built an inventory of recognized manifests, community files, CI workflows, and secret names.
Encoded guidance for the repository description, homepage, topics, and default branch.
Designed safe local preparation steps and remote authorization boundaries.
Added read-back verification and partial-success reporting.
outcomes: Agents can identify the gaps between a working codebase and a publicly ready repository.
Community and CI materials are prepared from facts about the project.
Proposed repository metadata reflects what the project actually is.
A repository is created or configured only when authorized, and the resulting state is verified.

summary: An agent skill that adds or updates one verified Agent Skill entry in an explicitly identified local Skillfolio catalog.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: Adding a skill to a catalog touches several consumers that duplicate its data, such as README indexes and the sitemap. It can also import stale package or repository facts, or treat a request to "publish" as permission to deploy. Either mistake breaks the catalog or makes an external change nobody approved.
constraints: Catalog schemas and the consumers that read them vary between target apps.
Repository, package, version, and compatibility facts must be verified against primary sources.
Editing the local catalog does not authorize a commit, push, npm publication, pull request, or deployment.

architecture.summary: The skill resolves the skill's identity from public package and repository evidence, then traces the target app's schema and every consumer of the catalog. A Python entry validator and the repository's own format, type, test, build, and sitemap checks decide whether the change is complete.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: Source resolution establishes the skill's canonical identity from public package and repository evidence.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: Schema and consumer tracing finds how the target app stores the catalog and every place that reads it.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: A Python entry validator runs alongside the repository's own format, type-check, test, build, and sitemap gates.

decisions.title: Discover the live catalog schema
decisions.detail: Schemas differ between target apps, so an assumed shape could produce entries that look valid but do not render. Reading the current schema costs a step on every run.

decisions.title: Change one entry and trace its consumers
decisions.detail: Limiting each run to a single entry keeps the change reviewable, and following every existing consumer keeps indexes and derived data in step with it.

decisions.title: Pair the validator with the app's own checks
decisions.detail: JSON shape alone cannot prove presentation or routing, so the heuristic validator is backed by the app's type-check, tests, and production build.

contribution: Defined the evidence and authorization rules.
Built the schema and consumer discovery workflow.
Implemented deterministic catalog-entry validation.
Integrated README index, sitemap, type-check, test, and production-build acceptance gates.
outcomes: Agents can resolve a canonical skill identity before editing the catalog.
Agents add or update a single valid entry.
README indexes and the sitemap stay aligned with the catalog.
Reports describe local completion without implying that anything was published.

summary: An agent skill for Codex and Claude Code that audits, creates, repairs, and verifies the large-image previews a website shows when its links are shared.
role: Agent workflow design and automation engineering
scope: Agent workflow, validation automation, and packaging
problem: A page can look correct in the browser while link-preview crawlers see missing or client-only metadata, an image that is too small or unreachable, or an old card the platform has cached. Implementation problems and cache problems need different fixes, and confusing them leads teams to rewrite correct metadata or wait on a cache that will never refresh.
constraints: Social platforms select and cache cards with proprietary rules that cannot be simulated or controlled.
Metadata must be visible to crawlers in the server HTML, and image URLs must be reachable remotely.
Dimension checks are deterministic only for PNG, JPEG, and supported WebP encodings.

architecture.summary: The skill inspects the repository and framework against a social-preview standard, then runs a deterministic checker over the raw HTML and image response. It preserves, repairs, or creates metadata and assets as needed, and verifies the result locally and on the deployed site.

layers.title: Skill workflow
layers.detail: Repository and framework inspection identifies how the app sets metadata and compares it with the social-preview standard.

layers.title: Automation
layers.detail: A deterministic HTML and image checker reports through exit codes 0, 1, and 2 so agents can tell outcomes apart.

layers.title: Verification
layers.detail: A preserve, repair, or create workflow is followed by verification on the local build and on the deployed site.

decisions.title: Separate implementation eligibility from cache symptoms
decisions.detail: Missing tags or a bad image are code problems, while a stale card is a platform cache problem that no code change fixes. Diagnosing them separately avoids fixing the wrong one.

decisions.title: Make the smallest framework-native repair
decisions.detail: Valid metadata is kept as it is, and changes use the framework's own way of setting tags, which keeps the diff small and consistent with the rest of the app.

decisions.title: Standardize new preview assets at 1200×630
decisions.detail: One size keeps new assets predictable. The checker still reads bytes, type, and dimensions from the file itself, because an extension can claim a format the file does not have.

contribution: Built auditing of the raw HTML, meta tags, and image response.
Implemented raster dimension validation and explicit exit codes.
Codified framework patterns and a social-preview standard.
Added installer, checker, and package-contract tests.
outcomes: Agents can tell a missing card apart from a cached one.
Incomplete, relative, or client-only metadata is repaired at its source.
A branded large-image asset is created only when one is needed.
Agents verify the local implementation and deployed crawler eligibility without promising a platform-specific layout.

summary: A versioned Bangladesh location dataset with census, postal, facility, ward, and infrastructure records, each traced to the government-published source it came from.
role: Data modeling, validation, and release engineering
scope: Provenance, transformation, validation, and distribution
problem: Bangladesh location records are spread across government sources that each use a different structure. That makes normalized lookup, provenance review, and repeatable machine consumption difficult for anyone building on the data.
constraints: Administrative boundaries, names, and facilities change over time.
Source coverage and confidence vary, and neither establishes authoritative identity or address truth.
Health, emergency, eligibility, routing, or legal use requires confirmation from a current authoritative source.

architecture.summary: Source and provenance manifests describe where each record comes from, and normalized records are governed by JSON Schema. JavaScript scripts validate those records and generate versioned JSON, JSONL, compressed, and SQLite releases with samples and documentation.

layers.title: Source records
layers.detail: Source and provenance manifests record where each dataset came from, what it covers, and its limitations.

layers.title: Transformation
layers.detail: Source data is normalized into geographic and facility records governed by JSON Schema.

layers.title: Release formats
layers.detail: Versioned JSON, JSONL, compressed, and SQLite outputs are generated from the same model, with samples and documentation.

layers.title: Validation
layers.detail: JavaScript scripts validate records against the schemas and produce deterministic release builds.

decisions.title: Keep lineage beside normalized data
decisions.detail: Storing source lineage and known limitations next to the records keeps uncertainty visible instead of hiding it behind a clean format.

decisions.title: Commit schemas and manifests, generate releases
decisions.detail: Reviewers read the schemas and manifests directly in the repository, while distribution files come from scripts. That adds release work but makes every change reviewable.

decisions.title: Publish several formats from one model
decisions.detail: Generating every format from a single model avoids maintaining divergent datasets that slowly disagree with each other.

contribution: Designed normalized geographic and facility schemas.
Assembled provenance and coverage manifests.
Built validation and deterministic release-generation scripts.
Documented responsible use, the update process, samples, citation, and source terms.
outcomes: Consumers can download structured location data as JSON, streaming JSONL, or SQLite.
Consumers can validate records against the published schemas.
Coverage and provenance limitations can be traced before the data is used.

summary: A Next.js starter that lets education organizations run a themed public website and content management from one shared codebase.

scope: Content architecture, authentication, and deployment
problem: Education organizations need familiar public information pages and publishing workflows. Cloning a whole codebase for each institution creates drift between the copies and makes every fix costly to maintain.
constraints: Three institution types and multiple layouts must share behavior without leaking content or theme between them.
MongoDB, Google OAuth and Drive, and Resend are optional services that each deployment has to configure.
Public pages must stay usable on read-only defaults when database-backed administration is absent.

layers.title: Content services

layers.title: Institution themes

layers.title: Integrations
layers.detail: MongoDB, authentication, Google Drive, and email adapters run behind an enforced server boundary.

decisions.title: Split identity tokens from layout composition
decisions.detail: Institution branding lives in tokens and page structure lives in layouts, so either can change without touching the other.

decisions.title: Resolve both themes on the server

Visitors see the configured branding and layout on shared routes.

summary: A release recovery for Book Heaven that separated a correct feature change from build-system failures, hardened the production build, and verified the deployed widget contract end to end.
role: Incident diagnosis, build engineering, and release verification
scope: Next.js build reliability, dependency compatibility, and Vercel delivery
problem: The SupportKori integration was correct in source and merged to main, but Book Heaven's Vercel production deployment failed before the new build reached visitors. The live site therefore looked as if the widget change were missing, even though the actual fault was in the delivery path. The recovery needed to identify each build blocker without weakening existing API contracts or treating a merged pull request as proof of a successful release.
constraints: The large Next.js application compiles many routes and integrations inside Vercel's finite build-memory envelope, and the default Node.js heap was exhausted during production validation.
The Stripe dependency used a caret range, allowing a newer release whose TypeScript contract expected a later API version than the application intentionally used.
Environment-backed providers initialize during route collection, so local checks had to distinguish absent production credentials from the build failures under investigation.
Acceptance required the exact script URL and data attributes to appear in public production HTML after a successful main-branch deployment.

architecture.summary: A four-stage recovery loop separated source correctness, deterministic production compilation, platform deployment, and public runtime verification so each failure could be diagnosed at the boundary where it occurred.

layers.title: Source contract
layers.detail: A root-layout Next.js Script component owns the exact SupportKori URL, account ID, message, color, and position.

layers.title: Build envelope
layers.detail: Prisma generation and Next.js compilation run with a 4 GB Node.js heap and two build workers to keep resource use predictable.

layers.title: Dependency contract
layers.detail: Stripe is pinned to version 20.1.0 so its types remain aligned with the API version selected by the application.

layers.title: Release proof
layers.detail: GitHub status, the Vercel preview, the production deployment, and the returned public HTML form a chain of release evidence.

decisions.title: Separate feature correctness from delivery health
decisions.detail: The widget implementation and the deployment pipeline were tested independently, preventing a stale production page from being misdiagnosed as a frontend defect.

decisions.title: Make the build resource budget explicit
decisions.detail: Increasing the Node.js heap and limiting parallel workers addressed the resource failure deterministically instead of relying on repeated deployment attempts.

decisions.title: Pin the dependency to the application's API contract
decisions.detail: Stripe stayed on the compatible 20.1.0 release rather than silently changing the application's API version to satisfy types from an unintended upgrade.

decisions.title: Verify the artifact visitors receive
decisions.detail: The incident was considered resolved only after Vercel reported a successful main deployment and the public response contained every required widget attribute.

contribution: Confirmed that the merged root-layout integration was correct while the public site was still serving the previous deployment.
Reproduced the production build and traced the failure through memory pressure and Stripe type-version drift.
Updated all production build paths with a 4 GB heap, limited Next.js to two build workers, and pinned Stripe to the compatible release.
Delivered the fixes through reviewed pull requests, then checked the Vercel preview, production status, and live HTML contract.
outcomes: The repaired main-branch build completed successfully on Vercel at the verified commit.
Book Heaven's public site now loads the exact SupportKori script with the required ID, message, color, and position.
Build behavior is less sensitive to heap exhaustion and excessive worker parallelism.
Stripe type compatibility can no longer drift beyond the selected API contract through an implicit minor-version update.
The release workflow now distinguishes code merged from deployment completed and production artifact verified.

screenshot.caption: The live Book Heaven beta was the final verification target: the fix was complete only when production served the intended widget contract.

summary: A visual generator and cacheable API that produces customizable animated typing SVGs for GitHub profiles, README files, and websites.

problem: Developers who want a typing animation in a GitHub profile or README usually have to edit SVG and CSS by hand and then host the result somewhere. That makes it slow to experiment with text, timing, or styling, and hard to share or reproduce a design someone else made.
constraints: Public embeds depend on the deployment staying available, because every image is generated on request.

summary: A small self-hostable Express service that increments a file-backed counter and returns the current value as a customizable SVG image for README files.
role: API design and backend engineering
scope: HTTP delivery, state management, and SVG generation
problem: README authors who want a number that changes cannot get one from Markdown alone, because Markdown cannot run JavaScript or call an API and render the result. The only dynamic thing a README can embed is an image URL, so a counter has to be a service that returns an image.

summary: A private, browser-only lookup that lets taxpayers check whether their Bangladesh TIN appears on a circulated NBR Risk-Based Audit selection list for AY 2023-24.
role: Data modeling, privacy design, and release engineering
scope: Client-side lookup, data provenance, and public distribution
problem: A list circulated as the NBR Risk-Based Audit selection for assessment year 2023-24, covering 72,342 returns, and searching it manually for one TIN is slow, especially on a phone. The obvious fix, a server-side search API, would send every person's tax identifier to another application server and its logs.
constraints: The data is a historical list, not a live audit or compliance status.
The claimed NBR provenance, accuracy, completeness, and redistribution rights have not been established.
Because the dataset ships to the browser, the records themselves are retrievable by anyone, even though lookup queries stay on the device.

architecture.summary: A Next.js page fetches the static JSON dataset once per session and caches it in memory. Each search normalizes the input and runs an exact match in the browser, and there is no API that receives a TIN.

layers.title: Lookup interface
layers.detail: A responsive Next.js page accepts a TIN and shows the match state with its mapped details.

layers.title: Session dataset
layers.detail: The static JSON list is fetched once per session and kept in memory for every later search.

layers.title: Client-side matching
layers.detail: Input is stripped of formatting characters and compared by exact digits, with no TIN submission API behind it.

decisions.title: Perform lookup entirely in the browser
decisions.detail: The server never receives an entered TIN, so no tax identifiers reach application logs. The trade-off is that the full list is downloadable by anyone.

decisions.title: Normalize formatting but require an exact digit match
decisions.detail: Spaces and formatting characters should not cause a miss, but a fuzzy match on a tax identifier would be worse than no match at all.

decisions.title: Show match state without interpretation
decisions.detail: A match displays only the mapped details, without inferring reasons, current status, or broader compliance that the data cannot support.

contribution: Converted the bundled list into a focused, responsive lookup.
Implemented one fetch per session with in-memory caching and digit normalization.
Added privacy, provenance, and methodology warnings with guidance to verify through official channels.
Documented the deployment and the repository's missing tests, security policy, and license.
outcomes: Users can search the historical list quickly, including on mobile.
Typed TINs are never submitted to an application API.
A match returns only the bounded details mapped from the list.
Both matches and non-matches tell the user to confirm their status with current official sources.

summary: A bilingual, institution-configurable operations platform that keeps form definitions, immutable versions, assignments, progress, notifications, and audit history attached to one submission.

scope: Multi-tenant authorization, configurable workflows, and bilingual service delivery

Google OAuth, Neon, Resend, and Netlify depend on environment-specific configuration without moving credentials into source control.

constraints: Every academic and financial workflow must preserve organization isolation and granular role permissions.
Students and teachers share physical biometric devices even though they have different domain records and responsibilities.
Payments and other critical business records require audit history and recoverable soft deletion rather than destructive removal.
Bangla SMS campaigns and attendance alerts must respect provider limits, scheduling, batching, and delivery state.

Financial corrections and record removal retain audit evidence instead of erasing operational history.

Assessment and payment flows cross multiple services, redirects, session states, and expiry conditions that must recover predictably.
Patient-facing errors and progress states must remain clear without exposing internal healthcare or infrastructure details.

Movement capture handles more device, tenant, and lifecycle edge cases without silently recording invalid or stale state.
Feature configuration supports multiple healthcare programs while preserving a shared application foundation.
Operational warnings and recovery paths surface earlier, reducing avoidable failures during patient-facing clinical workflows.

summary: A human-in-the-loop clinical workspace for reviewing recorded movement frames and correcting AI-generated lines, angles, key points, and measurement values before results are saved.
role: Frontend architecture and modernization within the MyMedicalHub team
scope: Clinical review workflow, canvas geometry, legacy API integration, validation, error recovery, and automated testing
status: Private employer-owned clinical tool under active modernization
problem: Automated movement analysis can place measurement geometry on an imperfect frame or anatomical position. constraints: Measurement geometry must remain correct while media is scaled, points are dragged, and line types restrict movement to one axis.
The workflow depends on multiple tenant-specific legacy APIs and session values whose payloads can be missing, stale, or inconsistent.
Large video frames and rendered canvas images must be validated and processed without freezing the review interface.
Clinical reviewers need explicit unavailable, loading, validation, save, retake, and completion states rather than ambiguous canvas failures.

decisions.title: Preserve measurement semantics

Implemented frame selection, draggable line and angle correction, automated-analysis comparison, reference guidance, save, retake, and completion states.
Added unit, integration, and browser-oriented coverage for geometry, upstream mappings, API contracts, and critical review interactions.
outcomes: Reviewers can correct automated clinical measurements through a guided workflow instead of manipulating an opaque legacy canvas.
Typed domain models preserve line, angle, direction, and measurement semantics across load, edit, render, and save operations.
Malformed or unavailable upstream data produces explicit recovery guidance rather than partially initialized review state.
The modernized boundaries make geometry and API behavior independently testable while legacy services continue to operate.

summary: An agent skill for building or auditing an Android app from an existing web product, with every web capability traced to an explicit Android disposition.

constraints: Every web capability needs an explicit Android disposition and evidence trail.
Platform adaptation must preserve product behavior without forcing browser interaction patterns onto Android.
Deferred and unsupported capabilities must remain visible rather than disappearing from scope.

Parity claims rest on evidence rather than visual similarity alone.
